podcast.title: Academic Achievement
podcast.body: In 1982, Morello enrolled at Harvard University, from which he graduated with an honors Bachelor of Arts degree in political science. He managed to achieve decent academic marks despite dedicating up to eight hours at a time to guitar practice. "In 1982, Tom enrolled at Harvard and graduated with an honors BA in political science."

podcast.title: Academic Achievements and Political Leanings
podcast.body: Morello's political leanings were evident from high school, where he was sometimes considered an anarchist. He graduated with honors and went on to Harvard University, where he studied political science and earned a bachelor's degree in social studies. "Tom's politics have always leaned left, going as far as being a little anarchist at times even in high school. He graduated with honors and enrolled in Harvard as a political science student. You played in more bands there too, including one called Board of Education, which also featured a future Nobel Prize winner in chemistry."

podcast.title: Disillusionment with Politics
podcast.body: Morello briefly worked in the office of a U.S. Senator, an experience that greatly disillusioned him and led him to abandon any aspirations of a political career, choosing instead to focus on music. "For a while, he worked in the office of a US Senator, but what he saw really disillusioned him. He was never, after this, going to have a career in politics. Music was his thing, starting with a band called Lockup."

podcast.title: Diverse Ancestry and Political Roots
podcast.body: Tom Morello was born in Harlem. His mother is of Irish and Italian descent, while his father, Niggethi Najorroj, was from Kenya. His father participated in the Mau Mau uprising, an eight-year revolt against British colonialism, and later became Kenya's first ambassador to the United Nations in 1960. Additionally, a great-uncle on his father's side was the first president of independent Kenya, and another uncle became a cabinet minister. "Tom was born in Harlem. His mom was both Irish and Italian while his dad was from Kenya. Dad's name was Niggethi Najorroj. He participated in the Maumau uprising, an eight-year-long revolt against British colonialism."

podcast.title: Hip-Hop Influence on Guitar Style
podcast.body: Despite playing in bands that covered rock acts like Led Zeppelin, Bachman-Turner Overdrive, and Black Sabbath, Tom Morello was profoundly influenced by Run DMC and Public Enemy. This led him to develop a unique guitar style that involved scratching the strings, mimicking a DJ's turntable technique. "Although these bands covered songs like Led Zeppelin, Bachminton, Overdrive, and Black Sabbath, Tom was profoundly affected by run DMC in public enemy. That's how his guitar style developed, scratching the strings, like a DJ would scratch on a turntable."

xref.title: Joe Hill (1915) – Swedish IWW Songwriter, Coined "Pie in the Sky," Executed by Firing Squad; Father of the Modern Protest Song
xref.body: Joe Hill was a Swedish-born itinerant laborer and songwriter for the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), a socialist union founded in Chicago in 1905 that organized logging, mining, farm, and factory workers. Hill is credited with coining the phrase "Pie in the Sky." He was arrested and charged with the murder of two people in Salt Lake City, subject to a major media trial, found guilty, and executed by firing squad on November 19, 1915. He is considered the father of the modern protest song and has many fans in the rock world, including Tom Morello of Rage Against the Machine, who has organized a memorial in Joe's name, performed his songs, and released songs about him. "You can draw a straight line from Rage Against the Machine right back to the 1910s and Joe Hill."

xref.body: Rage Against the Machine experienced an "implosion" on October 18, 2000, when their singer, Zack de la Rocha, quit the band. Despite this, the remaining three members—Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, and Brad Wilk—decided to stay together and search for a new vocalist, leading to the formation of Audioslave. xref.title: Reunion for Coachella (2007) Driven by George Bush
xref.body: Despite significant animosity rumored between Zach de la Rocha and the other band members, and numerous rejected offers for reunion, Rage Against the Machine eventually reunited for the Coachella Music Festival in April 2007, following rumors in late 2006. According to Tom Morello, the catalyst for their reunion was the political climate under President George Bush, as the band felt compelled to "stand up and oppose what was going on with the U.S. domestically and internationally." "Well according to Tom Morello, it was George Bush. The time had simply come for a band like Rage to stand up and oppose what was going on with the U.S. domestically and internationally."

xref.body: Audioslave formed when the remaining members of Rage Against the Machine (Tom Morello, Tim Commerford, Brad Wilk) sought a new singer after Zack de la Rocha's departure. xref.title: Formation of the Band
xref.body: After Zach de la Rocha left Rage Against the Machine, the remaining instrumentalists (Tom Morello, Brad Wilk, Timmy C) considered finding a new singer for Rage but were ultimately connected with Chris Cornell by producer Rick Rubin. During their first rehearsals, the immediate chemistry led to the writing of 21 songs in 19 days, including "Exploder," "Light My Way," and "Bring 'Em Back Alive." The members were committed to forming a full band, not just a one-off project, aiming for their new work to be "the best thing" they had ever done. "The first time we got together, we just jammed together and we decided, well, let's just try writing some songs. And I think the first three days of rehearsal with Chris, we wrote, exploder, light my way, and bring them back alive."

xref.title: Tom Morello's Guitar Style
xref.body: By the release of The Battle of Los Angeles, Tom Morello had developed a highly unique guitar playing style. He was known for using numerous effects to create diverse sounds, but a key characteristic highlighted was "the space between the notes," where "short gaps of nothing between the notes often say more than riffs that don't have gaps," creating a powerful effect. "By this time, he had developed a very unique playing style. He used lots of effects to get lots of different sounds. But when you listen to Tom's playing, the thing that really gets me is the space between the notes."

xref.title: Tom Morello's Songwriting Philosophy
xref.body: In an interview with Alternative Press magazine, Tom Morello articulated his view on songwriting, stating his disinterest in merely "good songs" that prompt toe-tapping. He aimed to write "great songs" that could "destroy cops and set fire to the suburbs," reflecting the band's confrontational political stance. "A good song should make you want to tap your toes and get with your girl. A great song should destroy cops and set fire to the suburbs. I'm only interested in writing great songs."

xref.title: Unique Guitar Playing Style
xref.body: Ian, the band's guitarist, developed a unique, self-taught playing style that combines rhythm and lead parts due to being the sole guitarist. He achieves this by playing in drop D tuning, which allows him to play bar chords with one finger while doing leads with the others, describing it as "almost like piano playing." He was influenced by clean players like Andy Summers and Mark Knopfler, as well as Tom Morello and Kim Thayil, and consciously avoided traditional playing. His style is considered "the most unique in the world." "I ended up trying to do both when I became the sole guitar player in this band. And by doing that, I found like dropping to D, I could play, I could play bar chords with one finger and then do a bunch of leads with the other."
